title: TA9-24623
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXXXX, the claimant, alleges she is a citizen of the People's Republic of China (PRC). She claims refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 ALLEGATIONS

The claimant alleges that in 2009 she was introduced into Christianity by her boyfriend. She began attending underground church services XXXX, 2009 and attended regularly thereafter. On XXXXXX, 2009, the claimant was not in attendance at her regular church services because she was required to work. While at work, she received a telephone call from her boyfriend advising her that the underground church was raided by the Public Security Bureau (PSB). The claimant immediately went into hiding. She subsequently learned that three members of her house church had been arrested and that the PSB attended her home to arrest her. Fearing she would be arrested, the claimant used the services of a smuggler to leave China for Canada where she filed for refugee protection.
The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The reasons are as follows.

The determinative issue in this claim is the credibility of the claimant's oral and documentary evidence in regard to her identity as a Christian. In this regard, the panel finds the claimant is not a credible witness. The reasons for this decision are noted below. Credibility Arrest of Fellow Church Members and Pursuit of Claimant by the PSB

The claimant alleges that three of her fellow church members were arrested and each received multi-year sentences. The claimant's testimony in this regard runs counter to the country condition documents that will be demonstrated later in these reasons with the analysis of the Situation of Christians in Fujian Province. In this regard, the panel draws a negative inference.

The claimant also alleges that the PSB have attended her home on numerous occasions with the intent of arresting her. The claimant testified that on the first occasion, the PSB also searched her home. She also alleges that the PSB attended her home 3 days later and showed her parents a warrant for her arrest. Country condition documents2 indicate that a summons is generally left with or shown to family members when the police want someone to come to their headquarters. In addition, the summons is the documentary basis for the subsequent issuance of an arrest warrant if the person in whom they are interested does not respond to the summons. The documentary evidence states in part: An arrest warrant can only be obtained with the approval of county level and above public security organs upon the presentation of an "application for Arrest-Summons". The application will state clearly and support with credible evidence that a crime has been committed, the person to be arrested-summoned for interrogation has been connected to the crime, and the suspect is not likely to appear voluntarily or that a summons for interrogation has been executed with no success.

The claimant has testified that the second time the PSB showed up at her house they showed a warrant to her family. According to the claimant's allegation, the PSB would not have known that she was not at her residence when they attended. If a warrant was issued as the claimant has alleged, then according to the country documents, the PSB would have had to provide credible evidence that the claimant was not going to attend voluntarily. Furthermore, the claimant has not alleged that a summons was left for her at her home. It does not seem plausible that the PSB would be able to provide that credible evidence given that they had not yet determined if the claimant was at home. In this regard, the panel draws a negative inference.

The panel prefers the evidence of the China country documentation in regard to the issuance of arrest warrants as this information is provided by unbiased, independent sources with no interest in the outcome of any particular refugee claim.

The notes that the claimant has provided any persuasive evidence to support her allegation that she is being pursued by the PSB. The only evidence she has provided is her testimony and the allegations she has made in her Personal Information Form (PIF). Travel to Canada

The claimant alleged that she used the services of a smuggler to leave China and travel to Canada because she was being pursued by the PSB. She alleges that the smuggler provided her with a fraudulent passport and that he accompanied her to Canada. The claimant was asked a number of questions with regard to her knowledge of the travel documents she used to travel to Canada. The claimant testified that she did not know the fraudulent name that was used in her passport and did not know her fraudulent address. In addition, she did not know if the passport contained a visa or the purported purpose of her travel to Canada. She also testified that she did not know the name that the smuggler was using in his passport or the type of passport he was using. The only thing she could offer with respect to her knowledge of the passport she and the smuggler used was that they were a dark blue colour. She claims that the only instructions she received from the smuggler was "not to worry" about anything and that, he would look after things.

While the panel does recognize the need for the Board to be sensitive to the vulnerabilities of claimants traveling under false documents, it does not excuse the claimant for all her testimonial failings concerning her lack of knowledge of the identity she was allegedly traveling under. The fact that she claimed to be following instructions does not explain why she could not relate anything of significance about the identities she and the smuggler were traveling under. The panel finds it neither plausible nor credible that the claimant would not be aware of this basic information in the face of the obvious likelihood that she would be questioned about it in transit.

On the basis of the subsequent analysis on the Situation of Christians in Fujian Province and in the context of the findings and negative inferences drawn above, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities that the claimant's allegation that there was a raid on her house church and that three of her fellow church members were arrested and each received multi-year sentences is neither plausible nor credible. Having found that the claimant's testimony about the arrest and incarceration of her fellow church members is not credible, the panel further finds that the alleged raid on the claimant's house church did not occur. Identity as a Christian

The claimant alleges that her religious profile is that of a devout Christian believer. The claimant alleges that she experienced a religious conversion when living in China. She alleges that she willingly risked her personal safety and security and joined an underground church in XXXX 2008. She alleges her faith led her to experience miracles performed upon her by Jesus. The claimant testified that she reads the bible daily for approximately 30 minutes and that she prays everyday. The claimant further alleges that she attends church three times a week in Canada.

The claimant testified that she arrived in Toronto on XXXXXXXX, 2009 but that she did not begin going to church in Canada until March of 2010. The claimant testified that she did not immediately begin attending church in Canada because in was "winter and there was lots of snow." She also stated that she did not know English and that her landlord told her that church was far way. The panel rejects that claimant's explanation. The panel notes that the claimant was able to contact an immigration consultant and was able to find legal representation at least by the time she signed her Personal Information form on January 20, 2010. It is reasonable to expect that if she was able arrange for counsel shortly after arriving in Canada despite her limited English skills, she would have been able to locate and attend church without too much difficultly. In this regard, the panel draws a negative inference. In addition, the claimant alleges that she risked her personal safety to attend an underground church in China. It is reasonable to expect that given her alleged religious profile that she would have sought the very first opportunity to attend church in Canada particularly since she was free to do so without risk. In this regard, the panel draws a negative inference.

The claimant was asked a number of questions concerning her religious knowledge. While she was able to demonstrate some knowledge, it was clear however, that she did not have a deep or meaningful understanding. The claimant was asked about the Holy Trinity. She described the Holy Trinity as the Holy Father, Jesus and the Holy Spirit. She was asked if Jesus was God. She responded that he was not God but the son of God. She was asked if the Holy Spirit was God. After some hesitation and repeating of the question several times, the claimant responded that the Holy Spirit was God. The claimant failure to understand that Jesus is God is very troublesome. A fundamental belief of Christianity is that Jesus is God. In this regard, the panel draws a negative inference. The claimant was asked to explain the Holy Trinity. The claimant responded by saying that Jesus Christ is the creator of mankind and the world and that Jesus, his son, was sent to earth to save mankind. The claimant correctly identified the Holy Spirit as the protector of mankind. The claimant's testimony that Jesus Christ is the creator of mankind and the world is inaccurate. A fundamental belief of Christians is that God, described as God the Father or God the Creator within the Holy Trinity, is the creator of the world and mankind. The panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's failure to know this fundamental belief. In addition, it is clear that the claimant does not know that the Holy Trinity is a concept of three divine persons in one. This too is a fundamental belief of Christianity and the panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's failure to know this.

While the claimant was able to provide answers to most fundamental questions, it was clear she did not have a clear understanding of the concept of the absolution of sin as it relates to the crucifixion and death of Jesus. The claimant testified that the death of Jesus absolved mankind of both original and personal sin. Christians believe that the absolution of original sin only comes through baptism. While it is true that there are many individuals who consider themselves to be genuine Christians who may not have a well-developed knowledge of Christian beliefs, the panel must consider whether it is reasonable for the claimant not to be aware of this distinction. The claimant alleges she has been attending church services and bible study 3 times per week since March 2010 and that he has been reading the bible daily since June 2009. She claims to be the beneficiary of miracles bestowed upon her by Jesus and alleges that while in China she risked her personal safety to express her faith. It is reasonable to expect that given the alleged religious profile of the claimant; she would have a deeper and more substantial understanding of the core beliefs of Christianity. In this regard, the panel draws a negative inference.

Nonetheless, the claimant demonstrated some knowledge of Christianity however, that knowledge does not necessarily mean she is a genuine practicing Christian. The claimant produced a baptismal certificate and a letter from Rev. XX.3 The letter indicates that the claimant has been attending church since March 2010. These documents can only attest to the claimant's participation in church activities, they do not attest to her motivation. In this regard, recent case law4 indicates that a pastor's assessment of the genuineness of a person's faith cannot be substituted for the assessment that the panel is required to make. Given the foregoing, the panel gives little evidentiary weight to Rev. Ho's letter and the Certificate of Baptism in assessing the genuineness of the claimant's Christian faith.

While it is difficult to make a judgment regarding the genuineness of a persons' religious practice it is necessary in this case. In doing so, the panel considered the totality of the evidence available. Having previously found that the claimant's testimony concerning her alleged house church in China untrustworthy, the panel further finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant was not a Christian in China. The panel further finds that the claimant's allegation that she was a practicing Christian in China is not credible and was only made for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent claim.

Having found that the claimant was not a Christian in China, the panel must consider whether the claimant is a genuine practicing Christian in this country. There is a requirement for 'good faith' in making a refugee claim. In this regard, R.P.G. Haines, the Chairman of a refugee status appeal panel and A.G. Wang Heed, a member of the United Nations High Commission for Refugees stated in part: If there is no good faith requirement in the sur place situation, it places in the hands of the appellant for refugee status the means of unilaterally determining the grant to him or her of refugee status.5

In this regard, the panel cites the following from James Hathaway's The Law of Refugee Status with regard to "sur place" claims: An individual who as a stratagem deliberately manipulates circumstances to create a real chance of persecution, which did not exist, cannot be said to belong to this category.6The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities that this claim has not been made in good faith.

Having found that the claimant was not a genuine practicing Christian in China and having found that this claim has not been made in good faith, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, and in the context of findings noted above, that the claimant joined a Christian church in Canada only for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent refugee claim. In the context as noted above, and on the basis of the totality of evidence disclosed and in the context of the claimant's knowledge of Christianity, the panel finds that the claimant is not a genuine practicing Christian, nor would she be perceived to be in China. Situation of Christians in Fujian Province

Notwithstanding the foregoing determination, in the alternative, the panel has considered whether there is a serious possibility that the claimant would be persecuted if she returns to China and chooses to practice Christianity in an unregistered church. The panel is guided by the Country Condition Documents in evidence.7The claimant is from Fujian province. The panel notes the documentary evidence states that Fujian and Guangdong have "the most liberal policy on religion in China, especially on Christianity" (Executive Secretary 1 Sept. 2005a). (ibid.).8

I also note that though there were arrests of Christians documented in 2005, 2006, 2007 and 2008, none of these arrests were noted as being in Fujian province. In 2005, there were reports of house church crackdowns in the provinces of Shanxi, Henan, Hubei, Jiangxi, and Jilin and in May 2005, Chinese officials coordinated raids on 100 house churches in Jilin province [northeast China], arresting approximately 600 Christians.9 During the year, there were also reports of similar incidents in Hebei, Xinjiang, Beijing and Shanghai.10 The U.S. 2008 International Religious Freedom Report11 specifically reviews arrests of Christians in China in 2007 and 2008 and notes arrests of Christians in Beijing, the XUAR, Jilin province, Hebei province, Guangxi province, Gansu province and Shaanxi province. No mention is made of arrests of Christians in Fujian province in 2007 and 2008. A review of the most recent articles12 in the exhibits covering 2008 and 2009 has revealed that there have been arrests of Christians in Beijing, Jilin province, Xinjiang province, Guizhou province, Hubei province, Hebei province, Inner Mongolia, the XUAR, Henan province, Sichuan province, Shandong province, Zhejiang province, Anhui province, Jiangsu province, Yunnan province and Gansu province. However, there have been no such arrests in Fujian province. Documentary evidence submitted does not provide any recent evidence of arrests of Christians in Fujian province.

The Annual Report of Persecution by the Government on Christian Churches within Mainland China13 very specifically notes the arrests and incidents of persecution of Christians in China from January 2008 to December 2008, but no arrests occurred in Fujian province where the claimant is from. This report states that during 2008, the number of Christians persecuted in all of China was 2,027 and that the number of Christians arrested and detained was 764, of which 298 were church leaders, which accounts for 39 % of all people arrested and 15.7% of all people persecuted. I have reviewed all the documentary evidence submitted and find no evidence of recent arrests of Christians in Fujian province.

In her representations to the panel, counsel for the claimant quoted statistics from the China Aid Association's (CAA) 2011 annual report. Although this report was not put before the panel and was not introduced into evidence, the panel has considered it in making this determination. In particular, counsel for the claimant noted that the CAA report states that ten persons were persecuted in 2010. A review of the CAA report by the panel reviewed that one incident was reported at a Lianjiang County church. The reports states that three venues used for the church gatherings were closed and that one church staffer was detained. Although the report states that ten persons were persecuted, there is no information how these persons were persecuted or why the churches were sealed. In fact, it is not clear from the report if the church is a registered or an unregistered church. As such, the panel can give the report little weight in assessing the over risk of persecution of Christians in Fujian. What is clear, however, is that no one was arrested or sentenced for underground activities.

The panel has considered all of the documents submitted about the situation for Christians in China, specifically the articles and reports documenting arrests and persecution. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that if there were recent arrests of Christians in Fujian province, there would be some documentation of these arrests.

The principle asserted in Maldonado14 is that when a refugee claimant swears to the truth of certain allegations, a presumption is created that those allegations are true unless there are reasons to doubt their truthfulness. However, the presumption that a claimant's own testimony is true is always rebuttable and, in appropriate circumstances, may be rebutted by the failure of the documentary evidence to mention what one would normally expect it to mention.15

The panel is supported in this analysis by a recent Federal Court decision16 by Justice Crampton who found that it was reasonable for the panel to find that, if underground Christians faced a serious possibility of persecution in Fujian Province, it would have been documented. The decision goes on to find that the panel was not unreasonable to differentiate between the treatment of Catholics and underground Protestants in Fujian.

The panel concedes that China Aid Association (CAA) has stated in its report and letters that they have not documented all cases of persecution and religious repression occurring in every province in China, including Guangdong and Fujian. However, I note again that there has been no mention at all of recent arrests of lay Christians in Fujian province in any of the documentation regarding religious persecution in China and according to the latest U.S. Department of State International Freedom of Religion Report,17 the extent of religious freedom in China continues to vary widely within the country. That report notes that unregistered religious groups have continued to expand and that most Christian groups, the majority of which are not registered, no longer operate in strict secrecy18 and in fact carried out public activities including convening seminars, publishing materials, renting space for offices and events, and disseminating information on the Internet. Many unregistered religious groups also carried out social service work. Both registered and unregistered faith-based organizations ran clinics, homes for the elderly, orphanages and social centers.19 In some regions, government supervision of religious activity was minimal with registered and unregistered churches existing openly and receiving similar treatment by the authorities.20 In parts of the country, unregistered groups grew rapidly and authorities did not pressure them to register.21 The panel finds that the situation in Fujian province does not reflect what is happening in many other provinces where there have been arrests of ordinary Christians.

The British Home Office Report notes that there are fifty to seventy million Protestant Christians in China who practice without state sanction and that only twenty million practice their religion in state approved churches.22 That report also states that prayer meetings and Bible study groups held among friends and families need not register with authorities.23 As has been discussed, the supporting documentary evidence for the claimant's home province of Fujian indicates, the risk of persecution for practicing Christians is low. The panel recognizes that even if the evidence speaks of some harm that would qualify as serious, the panel must consider whether there is a serious possibility that the harm will actually come to pass. A statute, which outlaws the claimant's conduct or characteristic, may be in existence, and it may provide for unconscionably severe punishment for that conduct or characteristic, but this does not necessarily mean there is a serious possibility that the punishment will be inflicted on the claimant. The Supreme Court has emphasized that, in a determination as to whether the claimant's fear is objectively well founded, the relevant factors include the laws in the claimant's homeland, together with the manner in which they are applied. In this connection, the Court cited paragraph 43 of the UNHCR Handbook. 24

This leads the panel to determine, that the claimant is free to choose to worship in the Christian congregation of her choosing. The panel has chosen to rely on the documentary evidence because it originates from a variety of reputable independent sources, which would reasonably be expected to be knowledgeable with respect to the situation of Christians in Fujian. The documentary evidence is seen as reliable, probative, detailed information, so as to provide the panel with a thorough understanding of the situation of the Christian Church in Fujian province.

The panel has considered the documentary evidence and the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant would be able to practice her religion in any church in Fujian province if she were to return to her home in Fujian province in China and that there is not a serious possibility that she would be persecuted for doing so.

The panel is support in this decision by a recent decision by Mr. Justice Russell.25 While this decision concerns an alleged raid in Guangdong Province, the profile of Fujian province is virtually identical in terms of country document evidence concerning policies and actions concerning membership in underground Christian churches. In reaching his decision, Mr. Justice Russell cited Justice Crampton's decision in Nen Mei Lin26 concerning Fujian province in which the court stated that in the context of the significant detail in the documentation regarding the dates and locations of arrests and other steps taken to discourage Christian activity in China, it was reasonable for the Board to conclude that if persecution of members of underground churches occurred in Fujian province it would have been documented. In addition, Justice Lemieux in Jiang27 noted that the documentary evidence concerning Fujian province indicates there is a minimum of constraints on religious practice and people generally practice their religion freely.

Further, in Yu,28 Justice Zinn noted that the only evidence provided to the Board regarding an alleged raid was the claimant's own testimony. It was further noted that although the claimant in that case had been found to be credible in regard to his Christian identity and membership in a house church, there was documentary evidence before the Board that brought his evidence of the raid into question and lead to an inference that no such raid occurred.

In the more recent Federal Court decision in the case of Yao,29 Justice O'Keefe notes that "this Court has held on several occasions that the Board's finding that Christian may practice freely in Fujian province is reasonable."

On the basis of the totality of the evidence and the cumulative findings and negative inferences noted above, the panel finds that the claimant has not satisfied her burden of establishing a serious possibility that she would be persecuted or that she would be personally subjected to a risk to her life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture by any authority in the People's Republic of China.

The claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The Refugee Protection Division rejects her claim. (signed) "L. Favreau" L.
